title: Density
lead: A ton of feathers and a ton of bricks have the same mass, yet one makes a far bigger pile than the other, and the quantity that tells them apart is density, the mass per unit volume of a substance. This section defines density, tabulates it for the common solids, liquids and gases, reads that table for what a density says about the composition and the phase of a substance, and works out from it the mass of the water held behind a dam.
objectives: Calculate the mass of a reservoir from its density.
Compare and contrast the densities of various substances.
summary_html:
• Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance or object. In equation form, density is defined as $\krho = \frac{m}{V}.$
  • The SI unit of density is $\text{kg/m}^3$.
notes: The three problems the book leaves unkeyed, the flask of mercury, the coffee mug and the trash compactor, are left out.

figures.original_caption: A ton of feathers and a ton of bricks have the same mass, but the feathers make a much bigger pile because they have a much lower density.

exercises.prompt: Approximately how does the density of air vary with altitude?

answer.solution: The density of air decreases with altitude. Air is a gas, and Table 11.1 gives its density near the ground as $1.29\ \text{kg/m}^3$, about a thousandth of the density of water. The atoms and molecules of a gas are separated by large amounts of empty space, and how much space depends on how hard the gas is squeezed: near the ground the air is compressed by the weight of all the air above it, while high up there is less air overhead and the same mass of air spreads through a larger volume. So the density falls steadily as you climb, and it falls off approximately exponentially, each equal step upward taking away about the same fraction of what remains, until at the top of the atmosphere it fades into the near-vacuum of space. Section 11.4 returns to the atmosphere as a fluid whose density changes with height.

exercises.prompt: Give an example in which density is used to identify the substance composing an object. Would information in addition to average density be needed to identify the substances in an object composed of more than one material?

answer.solution: A jeweler can test whether a ring is pure gold by weighing it and measuring its volume, for example from the water it displaces, and dividing to find its density. Pure gold has a density of $19.32 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$ in Table 11.1; if the ring comes out near $15.8 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$ it is an alloy, and if it comes out near $8.4 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$ it is brass. The same test tells a granite pebble from a lump of lead, or a cork from a piece of polystyrene. For an object made of more than one material the average density alone is not enough. The average is a blend of the densities of the parts weighted by how much of each is present, so one measured number can be produced by many different combinations: a mixture of gold and copper and a mixture of silver and lead could both come out at the same average. To identify the substances you would need something more, such as knowing what one of the components is, knowing the proportions, or measuring another property of the object that does not blend the same way, for example its color, its hardness, or how it conducts heat or electricity.

figure.alt: A glass filled to the brim with water and ice cubes.

exercises.prompt: The figure shows a glass of ice water filled to the brim. Will the water overflow when the ice melts? Explain your answer.

answer.solution: No, the water will not overflow. Table 11.1 gives the density of ice as $0.917 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and that of water as $1.000 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$, so ice is less dense than water, which is why it floats with part of each cube standing above the surface. When a cube melts, its mass does not change, but the water it becomes has the higher density and therefore, by $V = m/\krho$, a smaller volume than the ice had: smaller by the ratio $0.917/1.000$, that is, by about 8 percent. That 8 percent is just the fraction of each cube that was above the surface, so the melted water fills exactly the volume the submerged part of the ice occupied, the level stays at the brim, and nothing spills. Section 11.7 shows why the two fractions agree: a floating object displaces its own weight of water, so the submerged part of the ice already holds back exactly the volume of water the ice will turn into.

exercises.prompt: An under-inflated volleyball is pumped full of air so that its radius increases by 10%. Ignoring the mass of the air inserted into the ball, what will happen to the volleyball's density?

options: The density of the volleyball will increase by approximately 25%.
The density of the volleyball will increase by approximately 10%.
The density of the volleyball will decrease by approximately 10%.
The density of the volleyball will decrease by approximately 17%.
The density of the volleyball will decrease by approximately 25%.
answer.hint: The mass stays the same while the volume of a sphere grows as the cube of its radius, so ask what $(1.10)^3$ is and what $\krho = m/V$ does when $V$ is multiplied by that factor.

exercises.prompt:
A piece of aluminum foil has a known surface density of 15 g/cm2. If a 100-gram hollow cube were constructed using this foil, determine the approximate side length of this cube.
  1. 1.05 cm
  2. 1.10 cm
  3. 2.6 cm
  4. 6.67 cm
  5. 15 cm

answer.solution: A surface density is a mass per unit area rather than a mass per unit volume, so the foil’s mass is its surface density times its area, in the same way that an ordinary density gives $m = \krho V$. Divide the 100 g of the cube by the 15 g/cm² of the foil to find the total area of foil the cube contains. A hollow cube is six square faces, so divide that area by six to get the area of one face, and the side length is the square root of the area of a face. Keep track of the units: grams divided by grams per square centimeter leaves square centimeters, and the square root of square centimeters is centimeters, which is what the options are written in. Only one of the five options comes out of this arithmetic; the others are what you get by forgetting the six faces or the square root.

exercises.prompt:
Four spheres are hung from a variety of different springs. The table below describes the characteristics of both the spheres and the springs from which they are hung. Use this information to rank the density of each sphere from least to greatest. Show work supporting your ranking.
Material TypeRadius of SphereStretch of Spring (from equilibrium)Spring Constant
A10 cm5 cm2 N/m
B5 cm8 cm8 N/m
C8 cm10 cm6 N/m
D8 cm12 cm10 N/m
Rank the densities of the objects listed above, from greatest to least. Show work supporting your ranking.

answer.solution: Each sphere hangs at rest, so the spring’s upward force balances the sphere’s weight, and Hooke’s law from Section 16.1 gives that force as the spring constant times the stretch, $F = kx$. The weight is therefore $kx$ for each sphere, and its mass is $m = kx/g$; since every sphere is divided by the same $g$, the ranking of the masses is the ranking of the products $kx$, with the stretch converted to meters. The volume of a sphere is $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, so a sphere of twice the radius has eight times the volume, which matters more here than the differences in mass. Divide each mass by its volume to get $\krho = m/V$, and put the four results in order. Sphere A, with the largest radius and the smallest product $kx$, sits at one end of the ranking, and sphere B, with the smallest radius and a large product $kx$, at the other; C and D share a radius, so their order is decided by $kx$ alone. Write the four densities out in kg/m³ and list them from least to greatest to show your work.

exercises.prompt: Gold is sold by the troy ounce (31.103 g). What is the volume of 1 troy ounce of pure gold?

answer.hint: Solve $\krho = m/V$ for the volume, $V = m/\krho$, and take the density of gold from Table 11.1 in g/cm³ so that the grams cancel.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the mass of a deep breath of air having a volume of 2.00 L? (b) Discuss the effect taking such a breath has on your body’s volume and density.

answer.hint: One liter is 1000 cm³, and Table 11.1 gives the density of air as $1.29 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{g/cm}^3$; the mass is $m = \krho V$.
answer.solution: (a) 2.58 g. (b) The volume of your body increases by the volume of air you inhale. The average density of your body decreases when you take a deep breath, because the density of air is substantially smaller than the average density of the body before you took the deep breath.

exercises.prompt: A straightforward method of finding the density of an object is to measure its mass and then measure its volume by submerging it in a graduated cylinder. What is the density of a 240-g rock that displaces $89.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of water? (Note that the accuracy and practical applications of this technique are more limited than a variety of others that are based on Archimedes’ principle.)

answer.hint: The rock displaces its own volume of water, so the volume of the rock is the 89.0 cm³ that rises in the cylinder, and $\krho = m/V$.

exercises.prompt: (a) A rectangular gasoline tank can hold 50.0 kg of gasoline when full. What is the depth of the tank if it is 0.500-m wide by 0.900-m long? (b) Discuss whether this gas tank has a reasonable volume for a passenger car.

answer.hint: Find the volume of gasoline from $V = m/\krho$ with the density of gasoline from Table 11.1, and then divide by the area of the base, as the reservoir example multiplied an area by a depth.
answer.solution: (a) 0.163 m. (b) Equivalent to 19.4 gallons, which is reasonable.

exercises.prompt: A 2.50-kg steel gasoline can holds 20.0 L of gasoline when full. What is the average density of the full gas can, taking into account the volume occupied by steel as well as by gasoline?

answer.hint: The average density is the total mass over the total volume. The gasoline’s mass is $\krho V$ from Table 11.1, and the steel’s volume is its mass divided by the density of steel; add the two masses and the two volumes before dividing.

exercises.prompt: What is the density of 18.0-karat gold that is a mixture of 18 parts gold, 5 parts silver, and 1 part copper? (These values are parts by mass, not volume.) Assume that this is a simple mixture having an average density equal to the weighted densities of its constituents.

answer.hint: Take 24 g of the alloy, so that the parts are grams. Find the volume each metal contributes from $V = m/\krho$ with the densities of Table 11.1, add the three volumes, and divide the 24 g by the total.

exercises.prompt: There is relatively little empty space between atoms in solids and liquids, so that the average density of an atom is about the same as matter on a macroscopic scale—approximately $10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$. The nucleus of an atom has a radius about $10^{-5}$ that of the atom and contains nearly all the mass of the entire atom. (a) What is the approximate density of a nucleus? (b) One remnant of a supernova, called a neutron star, can have the density of a nucleus. What would be the radius of a neutron star with a mass 10 times that of our Sun (the radius of the Sun is $7 \times 10^8\ \text{m}$)?

parts.hint: The nucleus holds the whole mass of the atom in a sphere whose radius is $10^{-5}$ of the atom’s, so its volume is $(10^{-5})^3$ of the atom’s volume and its density is larger by the inverse of that factor.

Find the mass of the Sun from its radius and an average density of about $1.4 \times 10^3\ \text{kg/m}^3$, or take it as about $2 \times 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$; ten times that mass at the density of part (a) fills a sphere whose radius follows from $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$.
